one_liner: LLVM/Clang fork compiling Cilk fork-join C/C++ onto a work-stealing runtime; paper reports beating oneTBB, OpenMP and Cilk Plus runtimes.
what_it_does: OpenCilk is a compiler (this repository, an LLVM fork implementing the Tapir task-parallel IR) plus the Cheetah work-stealing runtime (OpenCilk/cheetah) and tools (Cilksan race detector, Cilkscale scalability analyzer). You write C or C++ with the Cilk keywords cilk_spawn, cilk_scope/cilk_sync and cilk_for, plus cilk_reducer types for reductions, and build with OpenCilk's clang -fopencilk; there is no library API to link into an ordinary GCC or MSVC build. It replaces a thread pool or task library such as oneTBB or OpenMP tasks for fork-join work, not std::thread-style job submission.
how_it_is_fast: The compiler keeps spawns and syncs visible in the IR (Tapir), so ordinary LLVM optimizations work across parallel control flow, and it lowers them to Cheetah calls whose fast paths ship as an LLVM bitcode ABI file that is linked and inlined into user code. Cheetah is a work-first, continuation-stealing scheduler in the Cilk-5 tradition: a per-worker deque guarded by the THE protocol, randomized victim selection, provably-good steals, per-worker fiber pools for the cactus stack, and adaptive thief sleep based on steal-success history (worker_sleep.cpp). cilk_for is lowered to recursive divide-and-conquer spawning (requires -O1 or higher).
when_to_use: Recursive or nested fork-join C/C++ code (divide-and-conquer, parallel loops nested inside parallel loops) where you control the compiler and can build with OpenCilk's clang.
You want a deterministic-by-construction programming model with tools: Cilksan to prove a run free of determinacy races and Cilkscale to measure work, span and parallelism before tuning.
Parallel reductions that must be deterministic (reducer hyperobjects) or repeatable parallel random numbers (DotMix DPRNG via -lopencilk-pedigrees).
Linux, macOS or FreeBSD on x86-64 or 64-bit ARM, including teaching and research settings (MIT 6.106 uses it).
when_not_to_use: You must build with GCC, MSVC or a stock Clang, or ship a library to users who do: Cilk keywords need the OpenCilk compiler, and Windows is not listed among supported systems.

Very fine-grained or low-parallelism workloads where little is stolen: in open issue #135 a 2^20-element recursive sum took about 600 us under OpenCilk versus about 120 us with ParlayLib par_do on two Xeon Platinum 8375C sockets (maintainers attribute it to scheduling overhead, NUMA and hyperthreading).
Projects relying on LTO or LLD LTO: open bugs #337 (LTO linker errors) and #313 (LLD LTO crash), plus #331 (cyclic dependency building shared libraries).
Job-queue or asynchronous task submission (fire-and-forget, futures, I/O-bound tasks): the model is strict fork-join, so a pool such as BS::thread_pool or concurrencpp fits better.
Code that needs the pedigree runtime: open issue #476 reports memory corruption on return from a steal with pedigrees.

integration.form: compiler toolchain (LLVM/Clang fork) plus runtime library (OpenCilk/cheetah); prebuilt release binaries for select systems
integration.dependencies: the OpenCilk compiler and its bundled Cheetah runtime; building from source needs a full LLVM build (infrastructure scripts provided)
integration.min_toolchain: OpenCilk clang with -fopencilk (OpenCilk 3.0 is based on LLVM 19.1.7; the dev/21.x branch carries the 4.0 release candidates); cilk_for needs -O1 or higher
integration.platforms: x86-64 and 64-bit ARM on Linux, macOS (via xcrun) and FreeBSD per the README; Android beta in 3.0; Windows not listed
integration.thread_safety: Runtime schedules spawned tasks across CILK_NWORKERS workers; user code must be free of determinacy races (checkable with Cilksan), reducers give race-free reductions
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the same Cilk source can be lowered to other runtimes, but replacing oneTBB or OpenMP code means rewriting it with Cilk keywords and switching compilers

gotchas: The paper's oneTBB and OpenMP baselines are not native TBB or OpenMP programs: the same Cilk source is lowered by OpenCilk's Tapir back ends to each runtime, so the comparison measures schedulers under OpenCilk's own front end. In dev/21.x the Tapir targets are Serial, Cheetah, CilkPlus, Lambda, OMPTask, OpenCilk and Qthreads; no oneTBB target ships, and the generic Lambda ABI needs an external bitcode ABI file, so the oneTBB comparison cannot be rerun from this repository alone.
A standalone CMake build of OpenCilk/cheetah defaults to CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug with all assertions enabled (cheetah README); benchmark against a Release build.

C++ exceptions are supported, but open issue #347 says out-of-order exceptions may call std::terminate, and several compiler crashes in Cilk exception handling and taskframe logic were fixed only recently (#483, #484, Aug 2026 commits).
Maintainers note in issue #135 that cilk_for with a reducer currently vectorizes poorly, so a reducer-based loop can be slower than a hand-written spawn tree.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick OpenCilk over library schedulers such as citor, Lace or Fork Union when you can adopt its compiler and want language-level fork-join with race detection, scalability analysis and deterministic reducers; prefer a library sibling (citor, Fork Union, Taskflow-style pools) when you must stay on a stock GCC, Clang or MSVC toolchain or need non-fork-join task graphs.
verified_claims_summary: The PPoPP 2023 paper by the project's authors reports the OpenCilk runtime faster than the Cilk Plus, OpenMP and oneTBB runtimes by a geometric mean of 4%-26% on 1 core and 10%-120% on 48 cores across 15 Cilk benchmark programs, all compiled by OpenCilk and lowered to each runtime; the paper was unreachable here (DSpace, ACM, scispace, NSF PAR and the conference site all failed DNS), so the per-runtime split, CPU model and flags remain unseen, and the only independent data opened (issue #135) shows OpenCilk slower than ParlayLib on a fine-grained 2^20 sum.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-17 on dev/21.x, OpenCilk 3.0 released on LLVM 19.1.7, 4.0 release candidates out) with 22 open issues; the compiler is an LLVM fork under Apache-2.0 with LLVM exception plus MIT for OpenCilk changes, so usable but only as a whole toolchain, not as code to vendor.
